question: How do I get HOA approval for new flooring in my Sarasota condo?
title: How to Get HOA Approval for Sarasota Condo Flooring
h1: How Do You Get HOA Approval for New Flooring in a Sarasota Condo?
description: Most Sarasota condo boards want spec sheets, an acoustic test report, and proof of insurance. Siesta Dunes requires IIC 50 and bans floating floors.
capsule: Most Sarasota-area condo boards want a renovation application with flooring and underlayment spec sheets, an acoustic test report, and installer insurance certificates before they approve a job. Siesta Dunes, for example, requires an underlayment rated at least IIC 50 under every hard floor above the first floor and prohibits floating floors entirely in those units.

sections.h2: What Most Renovation Applications Ask For
sections.html:
A typical Sarasota-area condo application asks for the flooring and underlayment spec sheets, an acoustic test report for the assembly, your installer's certificate of insurance, and a proposed start and finish date. Some buildings also collect a refundable construction deposit that's returned once the work passes inspection.

None of that paperwork is optional if your building requires it; skip a document and the application usually just gets sent back, which costs you time more than anything else.

We recommend starting this process well before your target installation date. A renovation application can take a board several weeks to review, especially if it needs to go to a committee meeting rather than a quick management sign-off. Waiting until material is already ordered puts you in the position of storing flooring for weeks while paperwork moves through the process.

sections.h2: A Real Example: Siesta Dunes' Rules
sections.html:
Siesta Dunes on Siesta Key spells its requirements out clearly: units above the first floor need an underlayment rated at least IIC 50 under both carpet and hard flooring, management has to inspect the underlayment before the finished floor goes down, and floating floors are prohibited above the first floor entirely. It's one of the more specific examples we've seen, and it shows how much a single building's rules can go beyond the state code baseline of IIC/STC 50.

Every association writes its own version of this, so treat Siesta Dunes as an example of the level of detail to expect, not a universal rule for Siesta Key or Longboat Key buildings generally.

What's consistent across most buildings, whether it's a low-rise near downtown Sarasota or a high-rise on the Gulf, is that the sound rule applies specifically to hard flooring above ground level, not to a first-floor unit sitting on grade. Confirm which category your unit falls into before assuming a rule from the floor above yours applies the same way to your own.

The most common holdup is submitting a general product spec sheet instead of the ASTM E2179 test report for the exact flooring-and-underlayment combination. The second is missing insurance documentation for the installer. Both are easy to avoid if you gather the paperwork before you submit, rather than after the board asks a follow-up question.

We build all of this into the free in-home estimate, so you're not chasing documents separately from getting your quote.

We've also seen applications stall simply because the proposed start date landed during a building's scheduled elevator or roof project. Ask your property manager about any blackout dates before you lock in a schedule with your installer.

sections.h2: How We Help You Get Approved Faster
sections.html: We provide a certificate of insurance on request, a written and line-itemized quote that separates underlayment from material and labor, and the manufacturer's test documentation for whatever flooring and underlayment combination we recommend. If your board's application has a specific format, bring it to the estimate and we'll fill in what we can on the spot. Our condo flooring approval checklist is a good starting point before you request the application from your property manager. See our condo flooring page for how this fits into a typical project from estimate to installation. We keep copies of past approval packages we've assembled for similar buildings on file, which sometimes helps us anticipate a specific board's preferences before your application even goes in. It's a small advantage, but it can shave a week or more off a process that otherwise involves a fair amount of back-and-forth.

faqs.q: Does every Sarasota-area condo require an acoustic test report?
faqs.a: Most do, but requirements vary building by building. Confirm with your specific association rather than assuming the state code minimum is all that's required.

faqs.q: Can I install a floating floor above the first floor at Siesta Dunes?
faqs.a: No. Siesta Dunes' published rules prohibit floating floors above the first floor and require a minimum IIC 50 underlayment under carpet and hard flooring alike, with a management inspection before the finished floor goes down.

faqs.q: What if my building doesn't collect a construction deposit?
faqs.a: Some do and some don't. It's not a statewide requirement, just a building-by-building policy, so check with your property manager rather than assuming either way.
